warmup.q: SELECT id FROM payments WHERE amount_cents > 90000 LIMIT 5 runs on a 100,000-row table with no index on amount_cents. About 1 row in 10 matches. Roughly how many rows does the sequential scan read?
options: All 100,000: the filter has to see every row before LIMIT can pick 5
About 50 or 60: the scan stops once LIMIT has its 5 rows
About 10,000: every matching row, of which LIMIT keeps 5
warmup.why: PostgreSQL's executor pulls rows. LIMIT asks the filter for a row, the filter asks the scan until a row passes, and after the fifth row LIMIT stops asking. With 1 row in 10 matching, the scan reads about 50 rows; the first Try it shows 62. Reading all 100,000 is what happens when every operator builds its whole result before passing it on. Exactly 5 would need an index that finds only matching rows.

sections.h: A plan is a tree of operators that pull rows one at a time
sections.html:
The last eight lessons were about where rows live and how indexes find them. Something has to run the query that uses them: the executor. Take SELECT id, amount_cents FROM payments WHERE amount_cents > 90000 LIMIT 5. The planner, lesson 10's subject, turns it into a plan: a tree of small operators that each do one job. A scan reads the table, a filter applies the WHERE clause, and a limit stops after 5 rows. EXPLAIN prints that tree with the root at the top and the scan at the bottom. This lesson is about how rows move through it.

Version 1 runs each operator to completion and hands its whole result to the next. The scan reads all 100,000 payments into a list, the filter builds a second list of the 10,000 that pass, and LIMIT keeps 5 and throws the rest away. It works, but it holds whole intermediate results in memory, which a 200-million-row ledger won't fit, and it reads 100,000 rows to answer a question about 5.

Version 2 turns the flow around. Every operator has the same three methods: open() to get ready, next() to return one row or null when there are no more, and close() to clean up. An operator gets its input by calling next() on its child. To produce a row, LIMIT calls the filter's next(), the filter calls the scan's next() until a row passes, and that row travels back up. After the fifth row, LIMIT returns null without calling its child again, and the scan never reads another row. Nothing is collected in a list: each operator holds one row at a time. This is the iterator model, also called the Volcano model after Goetz Graefe's research system from the early 1990s. PostgreSQL's executor works this way; its docs call it "a demand-pull pipeline". In Kotlin terms it is a Sequence rather than a List: payments.asSequence().filter { it.amount > 90_000 }.take(5) stops after five matches.

The stepper shows the calls going down and the rows coming up. In the Try it, the Seq Scan under the Limit returns 5 rows and discards 57, so it read 62 of the 100,000 rows. Without the LIMIT it reads them all and discards 90,001.

Some operators can't stream. A sort can't return its first row before it has seen every input row, because the last row read might sort first. So on its first next() it pulls its whole input, sorts it, then hands rows out one per call. Grouping with a hash table works the same way. These are called blocking operators, or pipeline breakers, and they are where memory limits (work_mem) and temp files come in.

sections.h: A nested loop join compares every pair
sections.html:
Now a join: each payment with its merchant's name. payments has 100,000 rows, merchants has 1,000, and the condition is m.id = p.merchant_id. A join is an operator with two children, the outer and the inner, and its next() must return the next matching pair.

Version 1 is the nested loop join, the two for-loops anyone would write. For each outer row, scan the whole inner input and return every pair whose keys are equal. In iterator terms, the join closes and reopens its inner child for every outer row. The cost is outer rows times inner rows: 1,000 x 100,000 = 100 million comparisons to produce 100,000 pairs. In the Try it, PostgreSQL, forced into this plan, put the merchants outside, scanned all of payments once per merchant (loops=1000), reported Rows Removed by Join Filter: 99900000, and took about 14 seconds.

The cost multiplies, so the fix is to make the inner side cheap. If the inner table has an index on the join key, the B+tree from lesson 4, then for each outer row the join does one index lookup instead of a full scan: three or four page reads, most of them buffer-pool hits, instead of 100,000 rows. That is the index nested loop join, and for a small outer side it is the best plan there is. In the Try it, joining 10 payments to their merchants does 10 index lookups and touches 10 merchant rows. A nested loop is also the only join that works for any condition, such as p.amount_cents > m.daily_limit_cents, because it compares every pair.

Reading the numbers needs one rule. EXPLAIN reports a node that ran several times per loop: actual rows=1.00 loops=10 means the inner index scan ran 10 times and returned 1 row on average each time, 10 rows in total. Multiply rows by loops to get the total. PostgreSQL 18 prints rows with two decimals because they are averages.

sections.h: A hash join reads each side once
sections.html:
For an equality join on two big inputs there is a better idea: build a lookup table. The hash join reads the smaller input completely into a hash table keyed on the join column. That is the build phase, and it happens before the first row comes out. Then it pulls rows from the other input one at a time and looks up each one's key: the probe phase. Each input is read once, so the work grows with outer plus inner rows: 101,000 row reads instead of 100 million comparisons. In the Try it the hash join takes tens of milliseconds where the nested loop took 14 seconds. The build side is a pipeline breaker; the probe side streams.

Two limits come with it. It only works for equality: a hash table answers "which rows have key 17", never "which rows have a key below 17". And the table needs memory. PostgreSQL allows a hash table work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier, 4 MB times 2 by default. If the build side doesn't fit, it splits both inputs into batches by hash value, writes the batches to temp files and joins them one pair at a time. EXPLAIN then shows Batches: 4 instead of 1, and the join still finishes, with extra disk traffic.

The third classic join is the merge join. If both inputs arrive sorted on the join key, walk them side by side, the way you merge two sorted lists, always advancing the side with the smaller key. Each side is read once and nothing extra is held in memory. It shines when the order is free, for example from a B+tree index scan, or when the result must be sorted anyway. When the order isn't free, it has to sort first: in the Try it the merge join sorts all 100,000 payments, spilling 2.5 MB to a temp file, and it is clearly slower than the hash join.

The figure puts the three side by side. The planner of lesson 10 chooses among them from its estimates of how many rows each side will have. The rough rule: index nested loop for a small outer side with an index on the inner, hash join for big unsorted equality joins, merge join when both inputs already come sorted.

sections.h: Vectorized execution pulls a thousand rows per call
sections.html:
The iterator model costs something on every row. For each row, each operator makes a call through an interface, which the CPU can't predict well when many operator types share one call site, and the WHERE clause is evaluated by walking an expression tree. For amount_cents > 9000 the comparison itself takes well under a nanosecond; the machinery around it takes many times that. On a query that touches 10 rows through an index nobody notices. On an analytics query that scans 100 million rows, it is most of the time.

The MonetDB/X100 researchers at CWI in Amsterdam measured exactly this in 2005 (Boncz, Zukowski and Nes). They ran TPC-H query 1, a scan of 6 million order lines that computes sums and averages, on MySQL 4.1: 26.6 seconds of CPU time. A profile showed the actual additions and multiplications took under 10% of it. One addition cost about 49 CPU cycles, because every function call computed a single value and the CPU could never overlap the work of two rows. A hand-written C program did the whole query in 0.22 seconds.

Vectorized execution changes the unit of work. next() returns a batch of values, stored by column, so a filter runs one tight loop over a plain array of amounts: no calls inside the loop, no expression tree, and code that the CPU can pipeline and the compiler can turn into SIMD instructions that compare several values at once. The cost of a call is paid once per batch instead of once per row. X100 ran query 1 in 0.50 seconds: over 50 times faster than MySQL and about twice as slow as the hand-written program. Its batches held 1,024 values, and the size matters: at 1 the MySQL overhead came back, around 1,000 was fastest, and above about 8,000 the batches no longer fit in the CPU cache and it slowed down again. DuckDB runs every query this way, with vectors of 2,048 values (STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE). Lesson 11 covers the column storage it pairs with.

In the Try it, the lab's demo runs the same filter and sum over 10 million payments three ways. In my run the row-at-a-time pipeline took 13.9 ns per row, batches of 1,024 took 1.9 ns, and a hand-written loop 0.33 ns. That last line is the next section's subject.

Why does PostgreSQL keep the iterator model? Its typical query finds a few rows through an index, where per-row overhead is noise, and the model keeps every operator small and easy to combine. DuckDB is built for the other end: scans over millions of rows. Your lab builds both: the iterator operators, then a vectorized filter that pulls batches of 1,024.

steps: Read VectorDemo.kt: the same sum(amount) WHERE amount > 9000 as a Volcano pipeline, as batches of 1,024, and as one loop.
From labs/, run the demo (no Docker needed). Predict the ratio between the Volcano and the batch times.

rows: 10,000,000   matching sum: 9,490,500,000
plan             cpu ms     ns/row
volcano           139.3      13.93

Here the Volcano pipeline needed about 7 times as long per row as the batch pipeline, and the plain loop was about 6 times faster again. Your numbers depend on your CPU, your JDK and what else the machine is doing (the demo prints the best of 5 runs to soften that), but the order stays the same. The batch version spends its time in two loops with no calls inside; the Volcano version makes a next() call per row per operator and evaluates the WHERE clause by walking an expression tree. sections.h: Compiled engines generate one loop per query, and pay to compile it
sections.html:
Batches are one way to stop paying the interpreter on every row. The other is to stop interpreting: generate code for this one query and compile it. Thomas Neumann's HyPer did this in 2011. Its compiler cuts the plan at the pipeline breakers from the first section and turns each pipeline (a scan, its filters, and the hash table or aggregate it feeds) into one loop that keeps the current row in CPU registers from start to end. No next() calls are left. It is the demo's plain loop, written by the database.

HyPer generated LLVM's intermediate code, which compiles in milliseconds; its first version generated C++ and waited seconds for the compiler. On query 1 of the TPC-CH benchmark, a grouped sum over the order lines of 12 warehouses, on one thread with everything in memory, HyPer took 35 ms. VectorWise, the product X100 became, took 98 ms, MonetDB 72 ms and a conventional disk-based system 4,221 ms. Compiling cost 16 to 41 ms per query with LLVM and 1.5 to 2.6 seconds with C++.

So which design wins? In 2018 Kersten, Leis, Kemper, Neumann, Pavlo and Boncz built both into one test system, with the same hash tables and the same parallelism, and found them surprisingly close on analytical queries. Compiled code executes fewer instructions, so it wins when a query computes a lot on data already in the CPU cache. Vectorized code keeps more memory reads in flight, so it wins when a query waits on large hash tables for joins and aggregation. SIMD helped less than expected, because most of the time goes to memory.

The cost that comparison sets aside is compile time. 16 ms is nothing next to a 10-second report and a lot next to a 2 ms lookup. PostgreSQL's JIT shows it. Since version 11 PostgreSQL can compile a query's expressions and row decoding with LLVM once its estimated cost passes jit_above_cost (100,000). In the Try it, a 100,000-row sum took 7.8 ms without JIT and 76 ms with full JIT optimization, 69 ms of it compiling. PostgreSQL 19, a release candidate in November 2026, turns JIT off by default.

Today's new engines are libraries you build a database from, and most are vectorized. Velox is Meta's C++ engine, used in more than a dozen of its systems: Prestissimo swaps Presto's Java workers for it, and Gluten runs Spark SQL on it. Apache DataFusion is a Rust engine built on the Arrow column format; InfluxDB 3 runs on it, and Comet uses it to run Spark plans natively. The Batch track meets them again where Spark runs.

refs.title: Neumann: Efficiently Compiling Efficient Query Plans for Modern Hardware (PVLDB 2011)
Kersten et al.: Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Compiled and Vectorized Queries But Were Afraid to Ask (PVLDB 2018)
Pedreira et al.: Velox, Meta's Unified Execution Engine (PVLDB 2022)

analogy: The iterator model is a pull-based assembly line, like a kanban system in a car plant. A station asks the station before it for one part only when it needs one, so nothing piles up between stations, and when the last station stops asking, the whole line stops. Vectorized execution moves parts in crates of a thousand instead of one at a time, so the walking between stations is paid once per crate. The analogy breaks at sorting and hashing: some operators must take in every part before they hand out the first one, which a good assembly line tries never to do and a database does all the time.
world: The N+1 query from an ORM is a nested loop join run by your service: for each of 500 orders, one SELECT ... FROM merchants WHERE id = ?, each a 1 ms round trip, so 500 ms, where one JOIN would let PostgreSQL hash-join in a few milliseconds. In Hibernate or Panache, fetch the association with a join (JOIN FETCH) or in one batch. Oracle has the same three join methods (nested loops, hash join, sort merge join) and its execution plans name them the same way, so the habit of reading rows and loops carries over. A Kafka Streams stream-table join is a hash join that never ends: the table side is the build side, kept in a local state store, and every stream record is a probe. And when a reporting query on the payments database is slow, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) tells you which node did the work, by its rows and loops, before anyone guesses.
mistake: The common mistake is fixing one slow join by turning off a join method for the whole server, such as enable_nestloop = off in postgresql.conf or a connection pool's init SQL. The one query gets faster, and hundreds of others that relied on index nested loops (fetch a few rows by key and join them) switch to hash joins that scan entire tables. People do it because the slow plan's nested loop looked guilty in EXPLAIN. Usually the real cause is a bad row estimate: the planner expected 10 outer rows and got 100,000, which lesson 10 covers. Fix the estimate (ANALYZE, extended statistics, a better index), or as a last resort set the flag with SET LOCAL inside that one transaction.

compare.title: One filter, two execution models (the lab's code)

a.label: Volcano
a.title: one row per call
a.html: class Filter(child: Operator, private val predicate: (Row) -> Boolean) : Unary(child) { override fun next(): Row? { while (true) { val row = child.next() ?: return null // a call per row if (predicate(row)) return row // another call per row } } }

b.label: Vectorized
b.title: 1,024 rows per call
b.html: override fun nextBatch(): Batch? { while (true) { val b = child.nextBatch() ?: return null // a call per batch val c = b.columns[column] val selected = IntArray(b.size) var n = 0 for (i in 0 until b.size) { // a tight loop, no calls if (c[i] > greaterThan) selected[n++] = i } if (n == 0) continue return Batch(b.columns.map { col -> LongArray(n) { col[selected[it]] } }, n) } }

compare.note: Both compute the same rows and both are pulled from above. The Volcano filter makes two calls per row and works on boxed values in a list; the vectorized one makes one call per 1,024 rows and spends its time in a loop over a LongArray, which the JIT compiles to fast machine code. The price is that every operator must work on batches, which makes LIMIT and joins more complicated to write.

worked.title: Trace a hash join on five rows

steps.say: The build side is three merchants, the probe side four payments, one with a null merchant. The join is HashJoin(build = merchants, probe = payments, buildKey = 0, probeKey = 1).

merchants (id, name):   (1, Acme)  (2, Bolt)  (3, Cord)
payments (id, merchant): (p1, 2)  (p2, null)  (p3, 1)  (p4, 2)

steps.say: open() runs the build phase: it drains the build side into a hash table from key to rows, then opens the probe side. Nothing has been read from payments yet.
steps.code: override fun open() { build.open() while (true) { val row = build.next() ?: break val k = row[buildKey] ?: continue // a null key never matches table.getOrPut(k) { mutableListOf() } += row } probe.open() } // table = {1: [(1, Acme)], 2: [(2, Bolt)], 3: [(3, Cord)]}

steps.say: Each next() first hands out pending matches for the current probe row; when there are none, it pulls the next probe row and looks its key up once.
steps.code: override fun next(): Row? { while (true) { if (matches.hasNext()) return matches.next() + probeRow!! val p = probe.next() ?: return null probeRow = p matches = p[probeKey]?.let { table[it] }?.iterator() ?: emptyList<Row>().iterator() } }

steps.say: Call next() four times. p2's null key skips the lookup. The fourth call pulls nothing new from the build side.
steps.code:
next() -> pulls p1, key 2 -> (2, Bolt, p1, 2)
next() -> pulls p2, key null, no lookup; pulls p3, key 1 -> (1, Acme, p3, 1)
next() -> pulls p4, key 2 -> (2, Bolt, p4, 2)
next() -> probe returns null -> null

steps.say: Count the work. The hash join read 3 build rows and 4 probe rows, and did 3 lookups. A nested loop over the same inputs would have examined 4 x 3 = 12 pairs. With 100,000 payments and 1,000 merchants that is 101,000 reads against 100 million comparisons.
steps.code:
hash join:    build 3 rows + probe 4 rows, 3 lookups
nested loop:  4 outer rows x 3 inner rows = 12 comparisons

lab.title: Build a Volcano executor with joins and a vectorized filter
steps: Read the top of Operators.kt: the Operator interface, Scan, and Unary, which opens and closes its child for you. Then read the Counting wrapper at the top of ExecutorTest.kt: it is how the tests see what each operator pulled.
Run the tests once. All 11 fail.
Write next() for Filter, Project and Limit. The pipeline and limit tests pass.
Write open() and next() for NestedLoopJoin, then for HashJoin. The join tests compare your hash join with your nested loop join on random data with duplicate and null keys.
Write BatchFilter.nextBatch() in Vectors.kt and run the tests until all 11 pass. Then run the demo from the last Try it again and look at its code next to yours.
hints: Limit.next() must check its count before it calls child.next(). If it calls first and checks after, it pulls one row too many, and the limit test counts the scan's rows.

In NestedLoopJoin, keep the current outer row in outer. When the inner side returns null, take the next outer row; if there is none, return null; otherwise right.close() and right.open() to rescan, and loop.
In HashJoin, a pending list of matches for the current probe row (an Iterator<Row>) is the whole trick: one probe row can match several build rows, and next() returns them one call at a time.
In BatchFilter, collect the passing positions first, then copy those positions of every column. Skip a batch where nothing passed: the tests check that you never return an empty batch.

drill.title: Write a nested loop join from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write open() and next() of a NestedLoopJoin(left, right, leftKey, rightKey) over the Operator interface (open, next(): Row?, close). It returns leftRow + rightRow for every pair with equal, non-null keys, and rescans the right side for every left row. Then say how many times the right side is opened for 100 left rows.

answer.html: private var outer: Row? = null override fun open() { left.open() outer = left.next() if (outer != null) right.open() } override fun next(): Row? { while (true) { val l = outer ?: return null // left side used up: done val r = right.next() if (r == null) { // right side used up for this left row outer = left.next() ?: return null right.close() // rescan it for the next left row right.open() continue } val k = l[leftKey] if (k != null && k == r[rightKey]) return l + r } } // 100 left rows: the right side is opened 100 times (once in open, then 99 rescans), // and it produces 100 x |right| rows in total.

recap: A plan is a tree of operators with open, next and close. Each next() pulls one row from below, so LIMIT stops the scan early and nothing is collected in lists. Sorts and hash builds are pipeline breakers that read all their input first.
A nested loop join costs outer x inner comparisons; with an index on the inner side it becomes one lookup per outer row, the best plan for a small outer side.

A hash join builds a table from the smaller side and probes it once per row of the other: about outer + inner work, equality only, batches on disk when the table outgrows work_mem. A merge join walks two inputs sorted on the key.

Row-at-a-time interpretation spends most of an analytics query on overhead: MySQL spent over 90% of TPC-H query 1 outside the arithmetic. Vectorized engines (X100, DuckDB, Velox, DataFusion) pass batches of about a thousand values and run tight loops over arrays.
Compiled engines (HyPer) generate one loop per pipeline and keep rows in registers. The two designs end up close; compiled wins on computation, vectorized on memory-bound joins and aggregation.
Compiling costs milliseconds per query, which can exceed the query itself: PostgreSQL's JIT made a 100,000-row sum slower, and PostgreSQL 19 turns JIT off by default.

explain.prompt: A teammate ran the same join twice, once with enable_hashjoin = off, and saw 50 ms against 9 seconds. Explain what the executor did differently in the two runs, using the iterator model and the row counts in the plans.
explain.answer: Both plans are trees of operators that pull rows with next(). In the fast run the hash join first pulled all 1,000 merchants from its build child into a hash table, then pulled the 100,000 payments one at a time and looked each one's merchant id up in the table: about 101,000 rows read and 100,000 lookups. In the slow run the planner could only use a nested loop. For each of the 1,000 merchants it closed and reopened the payments scan and compared every payment, so the inner scan ran 1,000 times (loops=1000) and 100 million pairs were examined, of which 99.9 million were thrown away (Rows Removed by Join Filter). The join produced the same 100,000 rows both times; the nested loop just did a thousand times more work to find them. A nested loop is only fast when the outer side is small and the inner side is an index lookup.

deeper.html:
Grouping and sorting. GROUP BY runs either as a hash aggregate (a hash table from group key to running totals, as in the Try its' HashAggregate) or as a sort followed by a group aggregate that streams through runs of equal keys. When the input doesn't fit in work_mem, a sort writes sorted runs to temp files and merges them, the external merge sort you saw as Sort Method: external merge. Hash aggregation spills batches the way the hash join does.

Parallel query. With parallel workers enabled, PostgreSQL runs copies of the lower part of a plan in several processes and a Gather node pulls their rows together; a hash join can even build one shared hash table. The Try its turned this off to keep the trees small. HyPer and DuckDB split work into small morsels of rows that idle threads pick up, which keeps all cores busy without planning the split in advance; Kersten and colleagues found that both compiled and vectorized engines scale well this way.

Push instead of pull. A compiled pipeline runs from the bottom up: the scan's loop pushes each row into the filter and on into the hash table, with no parent asking for it. Many vectorized engines push batches too. The result is the same set of rows; what changes is who holds the loop.

Memoize. Since PostgreSQL 14, a nested loop's inner side can sit behind a Memoize node, a small cache from join key to result. When many outer rows share a key, as 100,000 payments share 1,000 merchants, the inner lookup runs once per distinct key and every repeat is a cache hit. That is why the second Try it turned it off.
